body: Capital goods and EPC companies earn by executing projects from an order book. Revenue is recognised on percentage completion, and margin depends on bidding discipline, commodity pass-through clauses and execution speed. Product makers (transformers, switchgear, motors) earn a better margin than pure EPC and need less working capital. Key metrics: order inflow growth, order book/revenue (cover of 2–4x), book-to-bill, EBITDA margin, net working capital days, operating cash flow conversion, mix of fixed-price against variable-price contracts, and client mix (government, private, international). Cycle drivers: government capex (central capex rose from ~₹6 to ~₹11 lakh cr over FY21–26), private capex (utilisation above ~75% triggers it), power T&D (the ₹9 trn plan to 2032), Middle East hydrocarbon capex, and interest rates. Lead indicators: CMIE CapEx new project announcements, RBI capacity utilisation (OBICUS), Union/state budget capex spend (CGA monthly), CEA transmission bid pipeline, Tariff-Based Competitive Bidding awards, PGCIL capex. Winners (L&T, ABB, Siemens in 2003–07; KEC and Kalpataru in 2021–26) bid selectively, kept their balance sheets light and moved toward products. Losers were the 2007-era infrastructure EPCs (Lanco, GVK, Punj Lloyd, Gammon) that bought orders with low bids and debt and then died on working capital. Valuation: P/E 40–80x for product companies at the 2007 and 2024 peaks; pure EPC 15–25x. The 2007 peak took ~14 years to regain. Nov 2026: L&T Q2 FY27 order inflow was a record ₹1.48 lakh cr and its order book ₹8.54 lakh cr (+15% vs Mar 2026), but operating margins are under pressure. Traps: order book over cash flow, and peak-capacity product margins.

data.business_model: Project EPC (percentage completion) + engineered products; margin = bid discipline + execution + pass-through clauses.
data.current_state_nov_2026: L&T Q2 FY27: record order inflow ₹1,477 bn (+28%), H1 ₹2,557 bn (+22%), order book ₹8,53,514 cr (+15% vs Mar 2026), PAT +33%, op margins under pressure; FY27 guidance 10–12% revenue and order book growth. Transformer OEMs show peak-margin behaviour (see insight:transformer-peak-2026).
data.cycle_drivers: Govt capex budgets, private capex utilisation threshold, power T&D/renewable interconnection, data centres, Middle East oil capex, rates, commodity prices.
traps: Order book quality: slow-moving govt orders and fixed-price contracts
Rising receivables masked by strong P&L
Assuming 'capex cycle' at 60x lasts long enough
data.valuation: Product OEMs 40–80x P/E at peaks (Jan 2008, mid-2024), ~15–25x at troughs (2013, 2020). Pure EPC 12–25x P/E. BSE Capital Goods peak Jan 2008 regained only ~2021–22.
data.valuation_note: Historical valuation ranges and peak/trough dates come from general market history and were not re-verified against index factsheets this session. Treat them as unverified. Only the current-state figures are tied to the dated sources listed.
data.value_chain: Capex owner (govt/PSU/private/Middle East) -> EPC contractor -> equipment OEMs (transformers, switchgear, cables) -> sub-contractors -> commodities. Product OEMs in shortages (transformers 2023–25) capture the most margin, EPC captures less, and civil sub-contractors the least.
data.winners_vs_losers: Winners: selective bidding, negative/low working capital, product-heavy mix, strong parent technology (MNC listcos), conservative leverage. Losers: debt-funded EPC with aggressive bids (2007–12 infrastructure blow-ups), BOT/asset ownership taken on by EPCs, receivable build-up from state utilities.

title: Sector playbook: capital goods, EPC and power T&D
